title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 879–883 (Night 209, continuing nights-208), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 209 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Armānūs of the Ebony City rides out to meet the stranger camped outside his walls, takes the disguised Lady Budūr for a king's son, lodges her troops and, when she comes from the bath, offers her his throne and his only daughter, Ḥayāt al-Nufūs. Afraid to refuse and afraid to be found out, Budūr consents; the old king abdicates, the emirs swear to her as sultan, and she is wedded to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs. Two nights running she weeps verses for her lost husband, prays until the bride falls asleep and lies beside her untouched, while by day she rules justly, frees the prisoners and abolishes the tolls. The bride tells her father that her husband is wise and modest but only weeps and sighs, and the king resolves that if the third night passes in the same way he will depose and banish him; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and ninth night,
sentences.n: “The ninth after the two hundred”: al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ لَمَّا نَزَلَتْ عَلَى ظَاهِرِ مَدِينَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ لِأَجْلِ الِاسْتِرَاحَةِ أَرْسَلَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ رَسُولًا مِنْ عِنْدِهِ يَكْشِفُ لَهُ خَبَرَ هٰذَا الْمَلِكِ النَّازِلِ عَلَى ظَاهِرِ مَدِينَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-sitta Budūra lammā nazalat ʿalā ẓāhiri madīnati al-ābanūsi li-ajli al-istirāḥati arsala al-maliku Armānūsu rasūlan min ʿindihi yakshifu lahu khabara hādhā al-maliki al-nāzili ʿalā ẓāhiri madīnatihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-Lady Budūr, when she-halted upon (the) outside (of the) City (of) the-Ebony for-the-sake (of) the-resting, sent King Armānūs a-messenger from his-presence, (who) uncovers for-him (the) news (of) this king, the-one-halting upon (the) outside (of) his-city.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the Lady Budūr had halted outside the City of Ebony to rest, King Armānūs sent a messenger from his court to find out for him about this king who had camped outside his city.
sentences.n: The print has الآنبوس, a misprint for الآبنوس, corrected here: the nūn and the bāʾ have changed places, and the city is the City of Ebony, as at the end of the last night and again below. The print runs al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”, together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set. The night takes up the last sentence of the one before, where Budūr, travelling as Qamar al-Zamān, had pitched her tents outside the city. yakshifu lahu khabara, “he uncovers for him the news of”: a verb set straight after its noun with no conjunction describes it, “a messenger to find out”. al-nāzil, “the one halting, camping”, the active participle of nazala. The آ of الآبنوس is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهِمُ الرَّسُولُ سَأَلَهُمْ فَأَخْبَرُوهُ أَنَّهُ ابْنُ مَلِكٍ تَايِهٌ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ وَهُوَ قَاصِدٌ جَزَائِرَ خَالِدَانَ لِلْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilayhimu al-rasūlu saʾalahum fa-akhbarūhu annahu ibnu malikin tāyihun ʿani al-ṭarīqi wa-huwa qāṣidun jazāʾira Khālidāna li-al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: And-when arrived to-them the-messenger, he-asked-them, and-they-informed-him that-he (was the) son (of) a-king, straying from the-road, and-he (was) making-for (the) Islands (of) Khālidān, belonging-to King Shahramān.
sentences.i: When the messenger reached them he asked them, and they told him that he was a king's son who had lost his way, and that he was bound for the Khālidān Islands of King Shahramān.
sentences.n: tāyih, “straying, lost”: the print spells the participle of tāha with yāʾ, Middle Arabic for Classical tāʾih; it is kept. tāha ʿan al-ṭarīq, “to stray from the road”. qāṣid, “making for, intending”, takes its goal as a direct object. li-al-maliki, “belonging to the king”: li- marks the owner. Khālidān and Shahramān are diptote. Budūr's people give out the story she means them to: her husband is Qamar al-Zamān, son of Shahramān. The hamza of سألهم and the ئ of جزائر are printed.

sentences.t: فَعَادَ الرَّسُولُ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِالْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿāda al-rasūlu ilā al-maliki Armānūsa wa-akhbarahu bi-al-khabari
sentences.l: And-returned the-messenger to King Armānūs, and-informed-him of-the-news.
sentences.i: The messenger went back to King Armānūs and told him the news.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, Form IV, “to inform someone of”: bi- marks the matter told. Armānūsa is genitive after ilā, with the diptote's -a.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ نَزَلَ فِي خَوَاصِّ دَوْلَتِهِ إِلَى مُقَابَلَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Armānūsu hādhā al-kalāma nazala fī khawāṣṣi dawlatihi ilā muqābalatihi
sentences.l: And-when heard King Armānūs this speech, he-came-down among (the) chosen-ones (of) his-state to meeting-him.
sentences.i: When King Armānūs heard this, he rode down with the chief men of his state to meet him.
sentences.n: nazala here is “to come down, go out” from the palace or citadel. fī, “in, among”: in the company of. khawāṣṣ, plural of khāṣṣa, “the intimates, the select”; dawla, “state, reign”, and so “the court”: khawāṣṣ dawlatihi are his chief officers. muqābala, “meeting, going out to receive”, the verbal noun of Form III qābala.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَدِمَ عَلَى الْخِيَّامِ تَرَجَّلَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ وَتَرَجَّلَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ وَسَلَّمَا عَلَى بَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qadima ʿalā al-khiyyāmi tarajjalati al-sittu Budūru wa-tarajjala al-maliku Armānūsu wa-sallamā ʿalā baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: And-when he-came upon the-tents, dismounted the-Lady Budūr, and-dismounted King Armānūs, and-the-two-greeted upon each-other.
sentences.i: When he came up to the tents, the Lady Budūr dismounted, and King Armānūs dismounted, and they greeted each other.
sentences.n: qadima ʿalā, “to come to, arrive at”. The print puts a shadda on the yāʾ of الخيّام; the plural of khayma, “tent”, is khiyām, so the mark is odd, but it is the print's and is kept and read as it stands. tarajjala, Form V, “to dismount, go on foot”, from rijl, “foot”; the shadda of وترجّل is printed. sallamā ʿalā baʿḍihimā, “they greeted each other”, literally “upon part of the two of them”: the later language's way of saying “one another”.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَهَا وَدَخَلَ بِهَا إِلَى مَدِينَتِهِ وَطَلَعَ بِهَا إِلَى قَصْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhahā wa-dakhala bihā ilā madīnatihi wa-ṭalaʿa bihā ilā qaṣrihi
sentences.l: And-he-took-her, and-entered with-her into his-city, and-went-up with-her to his-palace.
sentences.i: He took her with him into his city and up to his palace.
sentences.n: The narrator calls Budūr “her”, though Armānūs takes her for a young man. dakhala bi- and ṭalaʿa bi-, “to go in with, go up with”: bi- is “with”, and the verb so becomes “to bring in, take up”. ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, the everyday later verb for climbing to a palace or an upper room.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ بِمَدِّ السِّمَاطَاتِ وَمَوَائِدِ الْأَطْعِمَةِ وَالْمَآكِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara bi-maddi al-simāṭāti wa-mawāʾidi al-aṭʿimati wa-al-maʾākili
sentences.l: And-he-commanded the-spreading (of) the-banquet-cloths and-tables (of) the-foods and-the-eatables.
sentences.i: He ordered the banquet cloths to be spread, with tables of food and every kind of dish.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes the thing commanded with bi-. madd, “stretching out, spreading”. simāṭ, “a long cloth or leather spread on which a feast is laid”; the print gives it the sound feminine plural, simāṭāt. mawāʾid, plural of māʾida, “table, tray of food”; maʾākil, plural of maʾkal, “food, dish”. The ئ of موائد and the آ of المآكل are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ بِنَقْلِ جَيْشِ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ إِلَى دَارِ الضِّيَافَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara bi-naqli jayshi al-sitti Budūra ilā dāri al-ḍiyāfati
sentences.l: And-he-commanded the-moving (of the) army (of) the-Lady Budūr to (the) house (of) the-hospitality.
sentences.i: And he ordered the Lady Budūr's troops to be lodged in the guest-house.
sentences.n: amara bi-, again “to command”, with bi- before the thing commanded. naql, “moving, transferring”. dār al-ḍiyāfa, “the house of hospitality”, the guest-house kept by a ruler for visitors and their followers. Budūra is genitive with the diptote's -a.

sentences.t: فَمَكَثُوا هُنَاكَ ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-makathū hunāka thalāthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: And-they-stayed there three days.
sentences.i: There they stayed three days.
sentences.n: makatha, “to stay, remain”. thalāthata ayyāmin, an accusative of time. The print writes ثلٰثة with a dagger alif for the long ā; it is kept.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَقْبَلَ الْمَلِكُ عَلَى السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَكَانَتْ دَخَلَتْ فِي ذٰلِكَ الْيَوْمِ الْحَمَّامَ وَأَسْفَرَتْ عَنْ وَجْهٍ كَأَنَّهُ الْبَدْرُ عِنْدَ التَّمَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aqbala al-maliku ʿalā al-sitti Budūra wa-kānat dakhalat fī dhālika al-yawmi al-ḥammāma wa-asfarat ʿan wajhin ka-annahu al-badru ʿinda al-tamāmi
sentences.l: And-after that, came the-king upon the-Lady Budūr; and-she-had entered on that day the-bath, and-she-unveiled from a-face as-though-it (were) the-moon at the-fullness.
sentences.i: After that the king came to the Lady Budūr. That day she had been to the bath, and had uncovered a face like the moon at its full.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, Form IV, “to come up to, approach”. kānat dakhalat, “she had entered”: kāna with a perfect gives the pluperfect, here without qad. dakhala al-ḥammāma, “she went into the bath”, the object taken directly. asfara ʿan, Form IV, “to unveil, uncover”: she has bared her face, and the radiance is her own. ka-annahu, “as though it were”: ka-, “like”, fused with anna. The rhyme falls on al-ḥammām / al-tamām, a touch of rhymed prose; and the badr, the full moon, is the singular of her own name, Budūr.

sentences.t: فَافْتَتَنَ بِهَا الْعَالَمُ وَتَهَتَّكَتْ بِهَا النَّاسُ عِنْدَ رُؤْيَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-iftatana bihā al-ʿālamu wa-tahattakat bihā al-nāsu ʿinda ruʾyatihā
sentences.l: And-were-enchanted by-her the-world, and-cast-off-all-restraint over-her the-people at seeing-her.
sentences.i: All the world was enchanted by her, and people lost all shame over her at the sight of her.
sentences.n: iftatana bi-, Form VIII, “to be infatuated with, enraptured by”: bi- marks what enchants. al-ʿālam, “the world”, here “everyone”. tahattaka, Form V, “to have one's veil torn, to be openly dishonoured”, of a lover: to lose all restraint and show his passion shamelessly; bi- marks the one he is mad for. al-nās takes a feminine verb, as a collective plural may. ruʾya, “seeing, sight”; the ؤ of رؤيتها is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَقْبَلَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ عَلَيْهَا وَهِيَ لَابِسَةٌ حُلَّةً مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ مُطَرَّزَةً بِالذَّهَبِ الْمُرَصَّعِ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika aqbala al-maliku Armānūsu ʿalayhā wa-hiya lābisatun ḥullatan mina al-ḥarīri muṭarrazatan bi-al-dhahabi al-muraṣṣaʿi bi-al-jawāhiri
sentences.l: And-at that, came King Armānūs upon-her, and-she (was) wearing a-robe of the-silk, embroidered with-the-gold, the-inlaid with-the-jewels.
sentences.i: Thereupon King Armānūs came to her, she being dressed in a robe of silk embroidered with gold set with jewels,
sentences.n: wa-hiya lābisatun, “while she was wearing”: a circumstantial clause, and the participle lābisa takes its object, ḥullatan, in the accusative like a verb. ḥulla, “robe, suit of fine clothes”. muṭarraza, Form II passive participle, “embroidered”, agrees with ḥulla; bi- marks the thread it is worked with. muraṣṣaʿ, “inlaid, set”, agrees with al-dhahab, and bi- again marks what it is set with: the gold thread is studded with gems.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا وَلَدِي اعْلَمْ أَنِّي صِرْتُ شَيْخًا كَبِيرًا هَرِمًا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā yā waladī iʿlam annī ṣirtu shaykhan kabīran hariman
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: O my-child, know that-I have-become an-old-man, great (in age), decrepit.
sentences.i: and said to her, “My son, know that I have become an old man, far gone in years and feeble.
sentences.n: yā waladī, “O my child”: walad is a child or son, and the king speaks to her as to a young man, though the narrator says lahā, “to her”. iʿlam annī, “know that I”, the usual opening for a piece of news. ṣāra, “to become”, takes its predicate in the accusative: shaykhan kabīran hariman, “an old man, aged, decrepit”, three accusatives in a row; haram is extreme old age.

sentences.t: وَعُمْرِي مَارُزِقْتُ وَلَدًا غَيْرَ بِنْتٍ وَهِيَ تُشْبِهُكَ فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿumrī mā ruziqtu waladan ghayra bintin wa-hiya tushbihuka fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli
sentences.l: And-my-lifetime, not I-was-granted a-child other-than a-daughter; and-she resembles-you in the-beauty and-the-loveliness.
sentences.i: In all my life I have been granted no child but one daughter, and she is like you in beauty and loveliness.
sentences.n: wa-ʿumrī mā …, “and in my life I have never …”: ʿumrī, “my lifetime”, stands loose at the head of a negative clause, the later language's “never in my life”. The print runs mā ruziqtu, “I was not granted”, together as one word, مارزقت; it is kept as set. ruziqa, the passive of razaqa, “to provide, bestow”: what God grants. ghayra bintin, “other than a daughter”, accusative as an exception. ashbaha, Form IV, “to resemble”. al-ḥusn wa-al-jamāl, “beauty and loveliness”, a stock pair. The print spells fī as فى.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا الْآنَ عَجَزْتُ عَنْ تَدْبِيرِ الْمَمْلَكَةِ فَهِيَ لَكَ يَا وَلَدِي
sentences.tr: wa-anā al-āna ʿajaztu ʿan tadbīri al-mamlakati fa-hiya laka yā waladī
sentences.l: And-I now have-become-unable from (the) managing (of) the-kingdom; so-it (is) for-you, O my-child.
sentences.i: Now I am no longer equal to ruling the kingdom, so it is yours, my son.
sentences.n: ʿajaza ʿan, “to be unable to, too weak for”. tadbīr, Form II verbal noun, “managing, governing”. fa-hiya laka, “so it is yours”: li- marks the owner. The آ of الآن is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ كَانَتْ أَرْضِي هٰذِهِ تُعْجِبُكَ وَتُقِيمُ بِهَا وَتَسْكُنُ بِلَادِي فَأَنَا أُزَوِّجُكَ بِهَا وَأُعْطِيكَ مَمْلَكَتِي وَأَسْتَرِيحُ أَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-in kānat arḍī hādhihi tuʿjibuka wa-tuqīmu bihā wa-taskunu bilādī fa-anā uzawwijuka bihā wa-uʿṭīka mamlakatī wa-astarīḥu anā
sentences.l: So-if is this my-land pleasing-you, and-you-stay in-it and-dwell (in) my-country, then-I marry-you to-her, and-give-you my-kingdom, and-rest, I.
sentences.i: If this land of mine pleases you, and you will stay here and make my country your home, then I will marry you to her and give you my kingdom, and take my rest.”
sentences.n: fa-in kānat … tuʿjibuka, “if it pleases you”: kāna with an imperfect, “if it is the case that”, and the two verbs after it, tuqīmu and taskunu, are joined to tuʿjibuka in the indicative. aʿjaba, Form IV, “to please”. aqāma bi-, Form IV, “to stay in”: bi- is “in”. sakana, “to dwell in”, takes the place as a direct object. zawwaja … bi-, Form II, “to marry someone to”: bi- marks the bride, and bihā is the king's daughter; the shadda of ازوّجك is printed. istarāḥa, Form X, “to rest, be at ease”. The closing anā, “I”, is set after the verb for weight: he himself will rest at last.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَقَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ بِرَأْسِهَا وَعَرِقَ جَبِينُهَا مِنَ الْحَيَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭraqati al-sittu Budūru bi-raʾsihā wa-ʿariqa jabīnuhā mina al-ḥayāʾi
sentences.l: And-lowered the-Lady Budūr her-head, and-sweated her-brow from the-shame.
sentences.i: The Lady Budūr bowed her head, and her brow broke out in sweat for shame.
sentences.n: aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi, Form IV, “to lower the head, look down in silence”: the verb takes the head with bi-. ʿariqa, “to sweat”. ḥayāʾ, “modesty, bashfulness, shame”. The hamza of برأسها is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا كَيْفَ يَكُونُ الْعَمَلُ وَأَنَا امْرَأَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat fī nafsihā kayfa yakūnu al-ʿamalu wa-anā imraʾatun
sentences.l: And-she-said in herself: How will-be the-doing, and-I (am) a-woman?
sentences.i: And she said to herself, “What is to be done, when I am a woman?
sentences.n: qālat fī nafsihā, “she said in herself”, that is, to herself. kayfa yakūnu al-ʿamalu, “how will the doing be?”, the later language's “what is to be done?”. wa-anā imraʾatun, “when I am a woman”, a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. The hamza of امرأة is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ لَمْ أَرْضَ وَسِرْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ لَمْ أَامَنْ فَرُبَّمَا يُرْسِلُ خَلْفِي جَيْشًا يَقْتُلُنِي
sentences.tr: wa-in lam arḍa wa-sirtu min ʿindihi lam āman fa-rubbamā yursilu khalfī jayshan yaqtulunī
sentences.l: And-if not I-consent and-I-go from his-presence, not I-am-safe; for-perhaps he-sends after-me an-army (that) kills-me.
sentences.i: If I refuse and go away from him, I shall not be safe: he may well send an army after me to kill me.
sentences.n: lam arḍa, “I do not consent”, the jussive of raḍiya after lam. sirtu, “I go”: after in, “if”, a perfect stands for the future. lam āman, “I shall not be safe”: amina, “to be safe, feel secure”, jussive after lam. The print spells the verb أامن, with a hamza on the first alif and a second alif after it, where the usual spelling is آمن with a madda; the letters are kept and read āman. rubbamā, “perhaps, it may be that”. yaqtulunī, “who will kill me”: an imperfect set straight after an indefinite noun describes it.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ أَطَعْتُهُ رُبَّمَا أَفْتَضِحُ
sentences.tr: wa-in aṭaʿtuhu rubbamā aftaḍiḥu
sentences.l: And-if I-obey-him, perhaps I-am-exposed.
sentences.i: And if I do as he says, I may well be found out.
sentences.n: aṭāʿa, Form IV, “to obey”. iftaḍaḥa, Form VIII, “to be exposed, disgraced”: on the wedding night her secret would come out. The answer of the condition, rubbamā aftaḍiḥu, has no fa-, which Classical would want there.

sentences.t: وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْتُ مَحْبُوبِي قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَلَمْ أَعْرِفْ لَهُ خَبَرًا
sentences.tr: wa-ayḍan faqadtu maḥbūbī Qamara al-Zamāni wa-lam aʿrif lahu khabaran
sentences.l: And-also I-have-lost my-beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and-not I-know of-him (any) news.
sentences.i: Besides, I have lost my beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and I know nothing of what has become of him.
sentences.n: ayḍan, “also, moreover”. faqada, “to lose”. lam aʿrif lahu khabaran, “I know no news of him”: li- marks the one the news is about.

sentences.t: وَمَالِي خَلَاصٌ إِلَّآ أَنْ أَسْكُتَ وَأَرْضَى وَأُقِيمَ عِنْدَهُ حَتَّى يَقْضِيَ اللّٰهُ أَمْرًا كَانَ مَفْعُولًا
sentences.tr: wa-mā lī khalāṣun illā an askuta wa-arḍā wa-uqīma ʿindahu ḥattā yaqḍiya Allāhu amran kāna mafʿūlan
sentences.l: And-not for-me (is) escape, except that I-keep-silent and-consent and-stay with-him, until decrees God a-matter (that) was done.
sentences.i: There is no way out for me but to keep quiet, consent, and stay with him, until God brings to pass what must be.”
sentences.n: wa-mā lī khalāṣun, “and I have no escape”: li-, “to, for”, marks the one who has; the print runs wa-mā lī together as one word, ومالي, kept as set. illā an, “except that”, with the subjunctive: askuta, arḍā, uqīma. The print writes illā as الآ, with a madda on the final alif; it is kept. ḥattā yaqḍiya allāhu amran kāna mafʿūlan, “until God decrees a matter that was to be done”, words from the Qurʾān (8:42 and 8:44), where kāna mafʿūlan is “that was bound to be”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ رَفَعَتْ رَأْسَهَا وَأَذْعَنَتْ لِلْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-sitta Budūra rafaʿat raʾsahā wa-adhʿanat li-al-maliki Armānūsa bi-al-samʿi wa-al-ṭāʿati
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Lady Budūr raised her-head, and-submitted to-King Armānūs with-the-hearing and-the-obedience.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr raised her head and gave King Armānūs her consent, with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then”: inna puts al-sitta Budūra in the accusative. adhʿana li-, Form IV, “to submit, yield to”: li- marks the one yielded to. bi-al-samʿi wa-al-ṭāʿati, “with hearing and obedience”, the stock phrase of assent: bi- is “with”. The hamza of رأسها is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ الْمَلِكُ بِذٰلِكَ وَأَمَرَ الْمُنَادِيَ أَنْ يُنَادِيَ فِي جَزَائِرِ الْآبَنُوسِ بِالْفَرَحِ وَالزِّينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-maliku bi-dhālika wa-amara al-munādiya an yunādiya fī jazāʾiri al-ābanūsi bi-al-faraḥi wa-al-zīnati
sentences.l: And-rejoiced the-king at-that, and-commanded the-crier that he-proclaims in (the) Islands (of) the-Ebony the-rejoicing and-the-adornment.
sentences.i: The king rejoiced at this, and ordered the crier to proclaim throughout the Ebony Islands a festival, with the streets to be decked out.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause. amara with a direct object and an, “to order someone to”. nādā bi-, Form III, “to proclaim, cry”: bi- marks what is cried. zīna, “adornment”: the decking of a city with lamps, hangings and silks for a festival. The city is the capital of the Ebony Islands, as the gardener said in the night before. The ئ of جزائر and the آ of الآبنوس are printed.

sentences.t: وَجَمَعَ الْحُجَّابَ وَالنُّوَّابَ وَالْأُمَرَاءَ وَالْوُزَرَاءَ وَأَرْبَابَ دَوْلَتِهِ وَقُضَاةَ مَدِينَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-jamaʿa al-ḥujjāba wa-al-nuwwāba wa-al-umarāʾa wa-al-wuzarāʾa wa-arbāba dawlatihi wa-quḍāta madīnatihi
sentences.l: And-he-gathered the-chamberlains and-the-deputies and-the-emirs and-the-viziers and-(the)-lords (of) his-state and-(the)-judges (of) his-city.
sentences.i: He gathered the chamberlains and the deputies, the emirs and the viziers, the great men of his state and the judges of his city,
sentences.n: ḥujjāb, plural of ḥājib, “chamberlain”, the officer who controls access to the ruler; nuwwāb, plural of nāʾib, “deputy, lieutenant”. The shadda in الحجّاب and in النوّاب is printed. arbāb al-dawla, “the lords of the state”, its grandees.

sentences.t: وَعَزَلَ نَفْسَهُ مِنَ الْمُلْكِ وَسَلْطَنَ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ وَأَلْبَسَهَا بَدْلَةَ الْمُلْكِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿazala nafsahu mina al-mulki wa-salṭana al-sitta Budūra wa-albasahā badlata al-mulki
sentences.l: And-he-deposed himself from the-kingship, and-made-sultan the-Lady Budūr, and-clothed-her (in the) suit (of) the-kingship.
sentences.i: and put himself down from the throne, and made the Lady Budūr sultan, and clothed her in the royal robes.
sentences.n: ʿazala, “to depose, remove from office”; ʿazala nafsahu, “he deposed himself”, abdicated. al-mulk, “kingship, royal power”, as against al-malik, “the king”. salṭana, a verb of the later language made from sulṭān, “to make sultan, enthrone”. albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the one clothed and the clothing. badla, “a suit of clothes”, a later word: badlat al-mulk, the dress of royalty.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَتِ الْأُمَرَاءُ جَمِيعًا عَلَى السِّتِّ بُدُورَ وَهُمْ لَايَشُكُّونَ فِي أَنَّهَا شَابٌّ ذَكَرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhalati al-umarāʾu jamīʿan ʿalā al-sitti Budūra wa-hum lā yashukkūna fī annahā shābbun dhakarun
sentences.l: And-entered the-emirs all upon the-Lady Budūr, and-they not doubting in that-she (was) a-youth, a-male.
sentences.i: All the emirs came in to the Lady Budūr, never doubting that she was a young man.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to come in to, enter the presence of”. al-umarāʾ takes a feminine verb, as a broken plural may. jamīʿan, “all together”, accusative. wa-hum lā yashukkūna, “while they did not doubt”, a circumstantial clause; the print runs lā yashukkūna together as one word, لايشكّون, kept as set, and its shadda is printed. shakka fī, “to doubt”: fī marks what is doubted. shābbun dhakarun, “a male youth”: the narrator keeps annahā, “that she”, while the court sees a man.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ كُلُّ مَنْ نَظَرَ إِلَيْهَا مِنْهُمْ جَمِيعًا يَبُلُّ سَرَاوِيلَهُ لِفَرْطِ حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra kullu man naẓara ilayhā minhum jamīʿan yabullu sarāwīlahu li-farṭi ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā
sentences.l: And-came-to-be every who looked at-her of-them all wetting his-drawers, for-(the)-excess (of) her-beauty and-her-loveliness.
sentences.i: And every one of them who looked at her wet his drawers, so overpowering was her beauty and her loveliness.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to, come to …”. kullu man, “everyone who”. balla, “to wet”; the shadda of يبلّ is printed. sarāwīl, “drawers, trousers”, a diptote. It is the storyteller's coarse hyperbole for desire so strong that the men spend themselves at the sight of her. li-farṭi, “because of the excess of”: li- gives the cause.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَسَلْطَنَتِ الْمَلِكُ بُدُورُ وَدُقَّتْ لَهَا الْبَشَائِرُ بِالسُّرُورِ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّهَا شَرَعَ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ فِي تَجْهِيزِ ابْنَتِهِ حَيَوٰةِ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā tasalṭanati al-maliku Budūru wa-duqqat lahā al-bashāʾiru bi-al-surūri wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyihā sharaʿa al-maliku Armānūsu fī tajhīzi ibnatihi Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: And-when became-sultan (she) King Budūr, and-were-beaten for-her the-glad-tidings with-the-joy, and-she-sat upon her-throne, began King Armānūs in (the) preparing (of) his-daughter Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: When King Budūr had been made sultan, and the drums of good news had been beaten for her in joy, and she had taken her seat on her throne, King Armānūs set about making ready his daughter Ḥayāt al-Nufūs for her wedding.
sentences.n: tasalṭana, Form V of the later verb salṭana, “to become sultan”. al-maliku Budūru, “King Budūr”: she now bears the title al-malik, masculine, while her verbs stay feminine. duqqat al-bashāʾir, “the glad tidings were beaten”: bashāʾir, plural of bishāra, “good news”, here the drums and music sounded to announce it; the ئ is printed. bi-al-surūri, “with joy”, and the shadda of بالسّرور is printed. kursī, “chair, throne”. sharaʿa fī, “to begin, set about”. tajhīz, Form II verbal noun, “equipping, making ready”: a bride's trousseau and wedding. The print spells the princess's name حيوٰة here, with the dagger alif over the wāw, the way the Qurʾān writes al-ḥayāh (الحيوٰة); it is read Ḥayāt.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ أَيَّامٍ قَلَائِلَ أَدْخَلُوا السِّتَّ بُدُورَ عَلَى حَيَوٰةِ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda ayyāmin qalāʾila adkhalū al-sitta Budūra ʿalā Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: And-after days few, they-brought-in the-Lady Budūr upon Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: And after a few days they brought the Lady Budūr in to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs as her bridegroom.
sentences.n: qalāʾil, plural of qalīl, “few”, a diptote, so genitive with -a. adkhala ʿalā, Form IV, “to bring someone in to”: the phrase for bringing a bridegroom in to his bride on the wedding night. The ئ of قلائل is printed.

sentences.t: فَكَانَتَا كَأَنَّهُمَا قَمَرَانِ فِي وَقْتٍ طَلَعَا أَوْ شَمْسَانِ قَدِ اجْتَمَعَا
sentences.tr: fa-kānatā ka-annahumā qamarāni fī waqtin ṭalaʿā aw shamsāni qadi ijtamaʿā
sentences.l: And-the-two-were as-though-they-two (were) two-moons (that) at a-time rose, or two-suns (that) had come-together.
sentences.i: The two of them were like two moons risen at one hour, or two suns come together.
sentences.n: kānatā, “the two of them (f.) were”, the feminine dual: here the narrator counts both as women. ka-annahumā, “as though they two were”: ka-, “like”, fused with anna. qamarāni and shamsāni, duals. fī waqtin ṭalaʿā, “at a time, they rose”, that is, at the same time. The rhyme falls on ṭalaʿā / ijtamaʿā.

sentences.t: فَرَدُّوا عَلَيْهِمَا الْأَبْوَابَ وَأَرْخَوُا السَّتَائِرَ بَعْدَ أَنْ أَوْقَدُوا لَهُمَا الشُّمُوعَ وَفَرَشُوالَهُمَا الْفَرْشَ
sentences.tr: fa-raddū ʿalayhimā al-abwāba wa-arkhawu al-satāʾira baʿda an awqadū lahumā al-shumūʿa wa-farashū lahumā al-farsha
sentences.l: And-they-shut upon-the-two the-doors, and-let-down the-curtains, after that they-lit for-the-two the-candles and-spread for-the-two the-bedding.
sentences.i: Then they shut the doors on the two of them and let down the curtains, having lit the candles for them and spread the bed.
sentences.n: radda al-bāba, “to shut the door”, literally “to turn it back”; ʿalā, “on”, the ones shut in. The shadda of فردّوا is printed. arkhā, Form IV, “to let down, loosen”; arkhawū, with the helping vowel u before the article. satāʾir, plural of sitāra, “curtain”; the ئ is printed. awqada, Form IV, “to light, kindle”. lahumā, “for the two”: li- marks those it is done for. The print runs farashū lahumā, “they spread for them”, together as one word, وفرشوالهما; it is kept as set. farsh, “bedding, what is spread”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ جَلَسَتِ السَّيِّدَةُ بُدُورُ مَعَ السَّيِّدَةِ حَيَوٰةِ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika jalasati al-sayyidatu Budūru maʿa al-sayyidati Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: And-at that, sat the-lady Budūr with the-lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr sat down with the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.n: al-sayyida, “the lady”, the Classical word, where the narrative has been using the colloquial al-sitt; both are titles of respect for a woman of rank. The print spells the name حيوٰة again.

sentences.t: فَتَذَكَّرَتْ مَحْبُوبَهَا قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَاشْتَدَّتْ بِهَا الْأَحْزَانُ فَبَكَتْ عَلَى فِرَاقِهِ وَغِيَابِهِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-tadhakkarat maḥbūbahā Qamara al-Zamāni wa-ishtaddat bihā al-aḥzānu fa-bakat ʿalā firāqihi wa-ghiyābihi wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: And-she-remembered her-beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and-grew-strong upon-her the-sorrows, and-she-wept over his-parting and-his-absence, and-she-recited, saying:
sentences.i: And she remembered her beloved Qamar al-Zamān, and her sorrows grew heavy upon her, and she wept for his parting and his absence, and recited:
sentences.n: tadhakkara, Form V, “to remember, call to mind”. ishtadda bi-, Form VIII, “to grow severe upon”: bi- marks the one it bears down on. bakā ʿalā, “to weep over, for”. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: an imperfect set after the verb describes how she did it; the verses follow.

sentences.t:
يَا غَائِبِيْنَ وَقَلْبِي زَائِدُ الْقَلَقِ * لَمْ يَبْقَ مِنْ بَيْنِكُمْ فِى الْجِسْمِ مِنْ رَمَقِ
وَكَانَ لِي مُقْلَةٌ تَشْكُو السُّهَادَ وَقَدْ * اَذَابَهَا الدَّمْعُ يَالَيْتَ السُّهَادَ بَقِي
لَمَّا رَحَلْتُمْ اَقَامَ الصَّبُّ بَعْدَكُمُ * لٰكِنْ سَلُوْا عَنْهُ مَاذَا فِى الْبِعَادِ لَقِيْ
لَوْلَا جُفُوْنِي وَقَدْ فَاضَتْ مَدَامِعُهَا * تَوَقَّدَتْ عَرَصَاتُ الْاَرْضِ مِنْ حَرَقِيْ
اَشْكُوْ اِلَى اللّٰهِ اَحْبَابًا عَلِقْتُهُمْ * لَمْ يَرْحَمُوا صَبْوَتِي فِيْهِمْ وَلَا قَلَقِيْ
لَا ذَنْبَ لِي عِنْدَهُمْ اِلَّا الْغَرَامُ بِهِمْ * وَالنَّاسُ بَيْنَ سَعِيْدٍ فِي الْهَوَى وَشَقِيْ
sentences.tr:
yā ghāʾibīna wa-qalbī zāʾidu al-qalaqi * lam yabqa min baynikum fī al-jismi min ramaqi
wa-kāna lī muqlatun tashkū al-suhāda wa-qad * adhābahā al-damʿu yā layta al-suhāda baqī
lammā raḥaltum aqāma al-ṣabbu baʿdakumu * lākin salū ʿanhu mādhā fī al-biʿādi laqī
lawlā jufūnī wa-qad fāḍat madāmiʿuhā * tawaqqadat ʿaraṣātu al-arḍi min ḥaraqī
ashkū ilā Allāhi aḥbāban ʿaliqtuhum * lam yarḥamū ṣabwatī fīhim wa-lā qalaqī
lā dhanba lī ʿindahum illā al-gharāmu bihim * wa-al-nāsu bayna saʿīdin fī al-hawā wa-shaqī
sentences.l:
O absent-ones, and-my-heart (is) exceeding (in) the-disquiet! * Not remained, from your-parting, in the-body any last-breath.
And-was to-me an-eye (that) complains-of the-sleeplessness; and-already * melted-it the-tear. O would-that the-sleeplessness had-remained!
When you-departed, stayed the-love-sick-one after-you; * but ask about-him what in the-separation he-met.
Were-it-not-for my-eyelids, and-already overflowed their-tear-courses, * blazed-up (the) open-spaces (of) the-earth from my-burning.
I-complain to God (of) beloved-ones (whom) I-clung-to-them; * not they-pitied my-yearning for-them, nor my-disquiet.
No fault (is) to-me with-them except the-passion for-them; * and-the-people (are) between happy in the-love and-wretched.
sentences.i:
O you who are gone, while my heart is restless beyond measure: * since you parted, not a breath of life is left in my body.
I had an eye that complained of lying awake, and now * its tears have melted it away: would that the wakefulness had stayed!
When you departed, the one who loves you stayed behind; * but ask what he has met with in the separation.
Were it not for my eyelids, whose tears have overflowed, * the wide plains of the earth would have caught fire from my burning.
To God I complain of the loved ones I gave my heart to, * who had no pity on my longing for them, nor on my unrest.
I have no fault in their eyes but my love for them; * and in love, people are either happy or wretched.
sentences.n: The print has مذا, a misprint for ماذا, corrected here: mādhā, “what?”, the object of laqī, “what he has met with”. The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed; Lady Budūr recites them to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs on the bridal night. The metre is basīṭ, and every line rhymes in -qi/-qī. ramaq, “the last breath of life, the least remnant of it”: min ramaqin, with the partitive min after a negative, “not a single breath”. muqla, “the eye”, properly the eyeball with lid and lashes. In the second line the sense is that tears have melted the eye away, so that even the sleeplessness it once complained of is gone: she would rather have it back. yā layta, “O would that”, set as one word in the print (يَالَيْتَ). baqī and laqī are baqiya and laqiya, “remained” and “met with”, cut to the rhyme. al-ṣabb, “the one who burns with love”, the poet speaking of himself. salū, “ask!”, the short imperative of saʾala, printed with a sukūn on its wāw. lawlā … tawaqqadat, “were it not for … (the earth) would have blazed”: the answer to lawlā here does without the usual la-. ʿaraṣāt, “open spaces”, plural of ʿaraṣa, the open courtyard or plain. shakā ilā, “to complain to”: the one appealed to takes ilā, the thing complained of is the direct object. The print's reading ʿaliqtuhum, “I clung to them, I fell in love with them”, is clear on the page only in part, the type being damaged there; it is the likeliest reading and is kept. ʿaliqa, “to cling to, be attached to”, is a stock verb for falling in love. lā dhanba lī, “there is no fault of mine”: lā of absolute negation with dhanb in the accusative. shaqī, “wretched”, the opposite of saʿīd, “happy”. The print sets a bare alif without hamza in اَذَابَهَا, اَقَامَ, الْاَرْضِ, اَشْكُوْ, اِلَى, اَحْبَابًا and اِلَّا, and writes fī as فِى in places; all are kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ السِّتَّ بُدُورَ لَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ إِنْشَادِهَا جَلَسَتْ إِلَى جَانِبِ السَّيِّدَةِ حَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ وَقَبَّلَتْهَا فِي فَمِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-sitta Budūra lammā faraghat min inshādihā jalasat ilā jānibi al-sayyidati Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi wa-qabbalathā fī famihā
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Lady Budūr, when she-finished from her-reciting, sat to (the) side (of) the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, and-kissed-her on her-mouth.
sentences.i: Then, when the Lady Budūr had finished reciting, she sat down beside the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and kissed her on the mouth.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to finish with”. inshād, the verbal noun of anshada, “to recite verse”. jalasa ilā jānibi, “to sit at the side of”: ilā, “to”, marks where she comes to sit. al-sayyida, “the lady”, the formal title, beside the colloquial al-sitt used for Budūr. The print spells the name Ḥayāt here with an ordinary alif (حياة), not the old spelling حيوٰة used earlier in this night. Budūr, in the tale, is disguised as her husband Qamar al-Zamān and has been married to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs in his name. The shadda of قبّلتها is printed.

sentences.t: وَنَهَضَتْ مِنْ وَقْتِهَا وَسَاعَتِهَا تَوَضَّأَتْ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تُصَلِّي حَتَّى نَامَتِ السِّتُّ حَيَاةُ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-nahaḍat min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā tawaḍḍaʾat wa-lam tazal tuṣallī ḥattā nāmati al-sittu Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: And-she-rose from her-time and-her-hour, performed-ablution, and-not she-ceased praying until slept the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: Then she rose at once and made her ablutions, and went on praying until the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs fell asleep.
sentences.n: min waqtihā wa-sāʿatihā, “from its time and its hour”, that is, “there and then”, a stock pairing. tawaḍḍaʾat, Form V, “she performed the ablution” before prayer; it follows nahaḍat without a wa-, the second verb carrying on the first. lam tazal tuṣallī, “she did not cease praying”: zāla with an imperfect, “to keep on”. The prayer keeps her from the marriage bed, which is the point: Budūr cannot let her bride find out who she is. The shaddas of توضّأت and تصلّي, and the hamza of توضّأت, are printed.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ مَعَهَا فِى الْفِرَاشِ وَأَدَارَتْ ظَهْرَهَا لَهَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalati al-sittu Budūru maʿahā fī al-firāshi wa-adārat ẓahrahā lahā ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-entered the-Lady Budūr with-her in the-bed, and-turned her-back to-her until the-morning.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr got into bed with her, and kept her back turned to her until morning.
sentences.n: adāra, Form IV of dāra, “to turn something round”; adāra ẓahrahu li-, “to turn one's back on”, li- marking the one turned from. The print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا طَلَعَ النَّهَارُ دَخَلَ الْمَلِكُ وَزَوْجَتُهُ إِلَى ابْنَتِهِمَا وَسَأَلَاهَا عَنْ حَالِهَا فَأَخْبَرَتْهُمَا بِمَارَأَتْ وَمَا سَمِعَتْهُ مِنَ الشِّعْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṭalaʿa al-nahāru dakhala al-maliku wa-zawjatuhu ilā ibnatihimā wa-saʾalāhā ʿan ḥālihā fa-akhbarathumā bi-mā raʾat wa-mā samiʿathu mina al-shiʿri
sentences.l: And-when rose the-day, entered the-king and-his-wife to their-(two's)-daughter, and-they-two-asked-her about her-state; and-she-informed-them-two of-what she-saw and-what she-heard-it of the-verse.
sentences.i: When day broke, the king and his wife went in to their daughter and asked her how she fared, and she told them what she had seen and the verses she had heard.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā or ilā, “to go in to” someone. The duals follow the two parents: ibnatihimā, “the daughter of the two of them”; saʾalāhā, “the two of them asked her”; akhbarathumā, “she told the two of them”. The verb dakhala before them stays singular, as a verb that comes first may. akhbara … bi-, Form IV, “to tell someone of”: bi- marks the matter told. bi-mā raʾat, “of what she saw”, set run together in the print (بمارأت), kept as set. mā samiʿathu mina al-shiʿri, “what of verse she heard”: min explains the mā, and the -hu on samiʿat returns to it. The hamza of سألاها and رأت is printed.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ حَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ وَأَبَوَيْهَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi wa-abawayhā
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and-her-two-parents.
sentences.i: So much for Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and her parents.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna … wa-ammā mā kāna, the storyteller's formula for leaving one thread and taking up another. abawāhā, “her two fathers”, is the dual of ab used for “father and mother”; here genitive, abawayhā.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ فَإِنَّهَا خَرَجَتْ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ الْمَمْلَكَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Budūra fa-innahā kharajat wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyi al-mamlakati
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) the-Queen Budūr, then-indeed-she went-out and-sat upon (the) throne (of) the-kingdom.
sentences.i: As for Queen Budūr, she went out and took her seat on the throne of the kingdom.
sentences.n: al-malika, “the queen”: the narrator now calls her queen, since Armānūs has handed his kingdom to the one he takes for Qamar al-Zamān. kursī, “chair”, and kursī al-mamlaka, “the throne”. fa-innahā answers ammā.

sentences.t: وَطَلَعَتْ إِلَيْهَا الْأُمَرَاءُ وَجَمِيعُ الرُّؤَسَاءِ وَأَرْبَابُ الدَّوْلَةِ وَهَنَّوْهَا بِالْمُلْكِ وَقَبَّلُوا الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَدَعَوْا لَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṭalaʿat ilayhā al-umarāʾu wa-jamīʿu al-ruʾasāʾi wa-arbābu al-dawlati wa-hannawhā bi-al-mulki wa-qabbalū al-arḍa bayna yadayhā wa-daʿaw lahā
sentences.l: And-came-up to-her the-emirs and-all (of) the-chiefs and-(the)-lords (of) the-state, and-they-congratulated-her on-the-kingship, and-kissed the-ground between her-hands, and-prayed for-her.
sentences.i: The emirs came up to her, with all the chief men and the officers of state; they congratulated her on her accession, kissed the ground before her, and called down blessings on her.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa ilā, “to go up to”, of courtiers coming before the throne; the verb is feminine to agree with the broken plural al-umarāʾ. arbāb al-dawla, “the lords of the state”, its great officers. hannaʾa … bi-, Form II, “to congratulate someone on”: bi- marks the occasion. The print's هنّوها is hannawhā, with the hamza of Classical hannaʾūhā dropped, as the spoken language does; it is kept. qabbalū al-arḍa bayna yadayhā, “they kissed the ground between her hands”, the courtly prostration before a ruler. daʿā li-, “to pray for”, li- marking the one blessed. The shaddas of هنّوها and قبّلوا, and the ؤ of الرؤساء, are printed.

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَتْ وَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ وَخَلَعَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ وَزَادَتْ فِي إِكْرَامِ الْأُمَرَاءِ وَأَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَإِقْطَاعِهِمْ وَالْجُيُوشِ
sentences.tr: fa-tabassamat wa-aqbalat ʿalayhim wa-khalaʿat ʿalayhim wa-zādat fī ikrāmi al-umarāʾi wa-arbābi al-dawlati wa-iqṭāʿihim wa-al-juyūshi
sentences.l: And-she-smiled, and-turned-towards them, and-bestowed-robes upon-them, and-increased in (the) honouring (of) the-emirs and-(the)-lords (of) the-state, and-their-fiefs, and-the-armies.
sentences.i: She smiled and turned to them graciously, bestowed robes of honour on them, and heaped yet more honours on the emirs and officers of state, and on their fiefs and on the troops.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, Form IV, “to turn towards someone, give them one's attention”. khalaʿa ʿalā, “to bestow a robe of honour on”, literally “to take off (a garment) onto”. zādat fī, “she increased in”, that is, did more of it than before. iqṭāʿ, “fief”, land granted to an officer for its revenue; wa-iqṭāʿihim, “and their fiefs”, and wa-al-juyūshi, “and the armies”, hang loosely on ikrām, as if the honouring took in the fiefs and the troops as well: she enlarged the fiefs and favoured the soldiers. The sense is clear though the syntax is slack.

sentences.t: فَأَحَبُّوهَا وَدَعَوْا لَهَا جَمِيعُ الْخَلْقِ بِدَوَامِ الْمُلْكِ وَهُمْ يَعْتَقِدُونَ أَنَّهَا ذَكَرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-aḥabbūhā wa-daʿaw lahā jamīʿu al-khalqi bi-dawāmi al-mulki wa-hum yaʿtaqidūna annahā dhakarun
sentences.l: And-they-loved-her, and-prayed for-her all (of) the-people for-(the)-lasting (of) the-kingship, and-they believing that-she (is) a-male.
sentences.i: They loved her, and all the people prayed that her reign might last, believing all the while that she was a man.
sentences.n: daʿaw lahā jamīʿu al-khalqi, “they prayed for her, all the people”: the verb is plural although its subject follows it, a construction Classical grammar avoids and the later language uses freely. daʿā li-X bi-Y, “to pray for X that Y”: li- marks the one prayed for, bi- the blessing asked. al-khalq, “creation, people”. wa-hum yaʿtaqidūna, “while they believed”, a circumstantial clause. dhakar, “male”. The shadda of احبّوها is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَتْ وَنَهَتْ وَحَكَمَتْ وَأَطْلَقَتْ مَنْ فِى الْحُبُوسِ وَأَبْطَلَتِ الْمُكُوسَ
sentences.tr: fa-amarat wa-nahat wa-ḥakamat wa-aṭlaqat man fī al-ḥubūsi wa-abṭalati al-mukūsa
sentences.l: And-she-commanded and-forbade and-judged, and-set-free whoever (was) in the-prisons, and-abolished the-tolls.
sentences.i: She gave commands and prohibitions and sat in judgement; she set free those who were in the prisons and abolished the tolls.
sentences.n: amarat wa-nahat, “she commanded and forbade”, the stock pair for exercising rule. The rhyme falls on al-ḥubūs / al-mukūs. ḥubūs, plural of ḥabs, “prison”. mukūs, plural of maks, “toll, market duty”, a tax the pious regarded as unlawful, so that abolishing it is the mark of a just ruler. The print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ قَاعِدَةً فِي مَجْلِسِ الْحُكُومَةِ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ اللَّيْلُ فَدَخَلَتْ إِلَى الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي أُعِدَّ لَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal qāʿidatan fī majlisi al-ḥukūmati ilā an dakhala al-laylu fa-dakhalat ilā al-makāni alladhī uʿidda lahā
sentences.l: And-not she-ceased sitting in (the) session (of) the-judging until that entered the-night; and-she-entered to the-place which was-prepared for-her.
sentences.i: She stayed seated in the hall of judgement until night came on, and then she went to the chamber that had been made ready for her.
sentences.n: qāʿidatan, “sitting”, a participle in the accusative as the predicate of lam tazal. majlis al-ḥukūma, “the session of judgement”: ḥukūma here is the act of judging, not “government”. ilā an, “until”, with a perfect. uʿidda, “was prepared”, the passive of aʿadda, Form IV of ʿadda; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَتِ السِّتَّ حَيَاةَ النُّفُوسِ جَالِسَةً فَجَلَسَتْ بِجَانِبِهَا وَطَقْطَقَتْ عَلَى ظَهْرِهَا وَلَاطَفَتْهَا وَقَبَّلَتْهَا بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-wajadati al-sitta Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi jālisatan fa-jalasat bi-jānibihā wa-ṭaqṭaqat ʿalā ẓahrihā wa-lāṭafathā wa-qabbalathā bayna ʿaynayhā
sentences.l: And-she-found the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs sitting; and-she-sat at-her-side, and-patted upon her-back, and-caressed-her, and-kissed-her between her-two-eyes.
sentences.i: She found the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs sitting there, so she sat down beside her, patted her on the back, caressed her and kissed her between the eyes.
sentences.n: wajada with two accusatives, “to find someone (doing something)”: jālisatan, “sitting”, is the second. bi-jānibihā, “at her side”: bi- is “at”. ṭaqṭaqa, a quadriliteral verb imitating the sound, “to tap, pat”, here a light pat on the back. lāṭafa, Form III, “to treat kindly, caress”. bayna ʿaynayhā, “between her two eyes”, on the brow. The shadda of قبّلتها is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: And-she-recited, saying these the-verses. Verse:
sentences.i: And she recited these verses:
sentences.n: anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: the second verb carries on the first. al-abyāt, plural of bayt, a line of verse. The last word, shiʿr, “verse”, is the print's own heading for the poem that follows, not part of the sentence.

sentences.t:
قَدْ صَارَ سِرِّيْ بِالدُّمُوْعِ عَلَانِيَهْ * وَنُحُوْلُ جِسْمِي فِى الْغَرَامِ عَلَانِيَهْ
اُخْفِى الْهَوَى وَيُذِيْعُهُ يَوْمَ النَّوَى * حَالِيْ عَلَى الْوَاشِيْنَ لَيْسَتْ خَافِيَهْ
يَا رَاحِلِيْنَ عَنِ الْحِمَى خَلَّفْتُمُ * جِسْمِيْ بِكُمْ مُضْنًى وَنَفْسِيْ بَالِيَه
وَسَكَنْتُمُ غَوْرَ الْحَشَى فَنَوَاظِرِيْ * تَجْرِيْ مَدَامِعُهَا وَعَيْنِيْ دَامِيَه
وَاَنَا فِدَاءُ الْغَائِبِيْنَ بِمُهْجَتِيْ * اَبَدًا وَاَشْوَاقِيْ اِلَيْهِمْ بَادِيَه
لِيْ مُقْلَةٌ اِنْسَانُهَا فِيْ حُبِّهِمْ * رَفَضَ الْكَرَى وَدُمُوْعُهَا مُتَوَالِيَه
ظَنَّ الْعِدَى مِنِّيْ عَلَيْهِ تَجَلُّدًا * هَيْهَاتَ مَا اُذُنِيْ اِلَيْهِمْ وَاعِيَهْ
خَابَتْ ظُنُوْنُهُمُ عَلَيَّ وَاِنَّمَا * قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِهِ اَنَالُ اَمَانِيَه
جَمَعَ الْفَضَائِلَ مَا حَوَاهَا قَبْلَهُ * اَحَدٌ سِوَاهُ مِنَ الْمُلُوكِ الْخَالِيَه
اَنْسَى الْاَنَامَ بِجُوْدِهِ وَبِعَفْوِهِ * كَرَمُ ابْنُ زَائِدَةِ وَحِلْمُ مُعَاوِيَه
لَوْلَا الْاِطَالَةُ وَالْقَرِيضُ مُقَصِّرٌ * عَنْ وَصْفِ حُسْنِكَ لَمْ اَدَعْ مِنْ قَافِيَه
sentences.tr:
qad ṣāra sirrī bi-al-dumūʿi ʿalāniyah * wa-nuḥūlu jismī fī al-gharāmi ʿalāniyah
ukhfī al-hawā wa-yudhīʿuhu yawma al-nawā * ḥālī ʿalā al-wāshīna laysat khāfiyah
yā rāḥilīna ʿani al-ḥimā khallaftumu * jismī bikum muḍnan wa-nafsī bāliyah
wa-sakantumu ghawra al-ḥashā fa-nawāẓirī * tajrī madāmiʿuhā wa-ʿaynī dāmiyah
wa-anā fidāʾu al-ghāʾibīna bi-muhjatī * abadan wa-ashwāqī ilayhim bādiyah
lī muqlatun insānuhā fī ḥubbihim * rafaḍa al-karā wa-dumūʿuhā mutawāliyah
ẓanna al-ʿidā minnī ʿalayhi tajalludan * hayhāta mā udhunī ilayhim wāʿiyah
khābat ẓunūnuhumu ʿalayya wa-innamā * Qamaru al-Zamāni bihi anālu amāniyah
jamaʿa al-faḍāʾila mā ḥawāhā qablahu * aḥadun siwāhu mina al-mulūki al-khāliyah
ansā al-anāma bi-jūdihi wa-bi-ʿafwihi * karamu ibnu Zāʾidati wa-ḥilmu Muʿāwiyah
lawlā al-iṭālatu wa-al-qarīḍu muqaṣṣirun * ʿan waṣfi ḥusnika lam adaʿ min qāfiyah
sentences.l:
Has-become my-secret, through-the-tears, open, * and-(the)-wasting (of) my-body in the-passion (is) open.
I-hide the-love, and-discloses-it, (on the) day (of) the-parting, * my-state; to the-slanderers it-is-not hidden.
O departing-ones from the-preserve, you-left-behind * my-body through-you wasted, and-my-soul worn-out.
And-you-dwelt (in the) depth (of) the-entrails; so-my-eyes, * flow their-tears, and-my-eye (is) bleeding.
And-I (am the) ransom (of) the-absent-ones with-my-heart's-blood * forever, and-my-longings toward-them (are) showing.
To-me (is) an-eye, its-pupil, in their-love, * refused the-slumber, and-its-tears (are) following-one-another.
Supposed the-enemies in-me, upon-it, endurance; * far-from-it! Not my-ear to-them (is) heeding.
Failed their-suppositions about-me; and-only * Qamar al-Zamān, through-him I-attain (my) hopes.
He-gathered the-virtues; not held-them before-him * anyone other-than-him of the-kings the-bygone.
He-made-forget the-mankind, by-his-bounty and-by-his-pardon, * (the) generosity (of) Ibn Zāʾida and-(the)-forbearance (of) Muʿāwiya.
Were-it-not-for the-lengthening, and-the-verse (is) falling-short * of (the) describing (of) your-beauty, not I-would-leave (any) of rhyme.
sentences.i:
My secret has been made public by my tears, * and the wasting of my body in love is there for all to see.
I hide my love, but on the day of parting * my state gives it away; it is no secret from the slanderers.
O you who have left the encampment, you have left behind you * my body wasted for your sake, and my soul worn to nothing.
You have made your dwelling deep within my breast; so my eyes * run with tears, and my eye bleeds.
I would ransom the absent with my very heart's blood, * forever; and my longing for them shows plainly.
I have an eye whose pupil, for love of them, * has refused all sleep, and its tears fall one upon another.
My enemies thought me hardened against it: * far from it! My ear pays them no heed.
Their guesses about me have come to nothing; it is only * through Qamar al-Zamān that I shall gain my hopes.
He has gathered virtues that no one before him * among the kings of old ever possessed.
With his bounty and his clemency he has made the world forget * the generosity of Ibn Zāʾida and the forbearance of Muʿāwiya.
Were it not that I would run on too long, and that verse falls short * of describing your beauty, I would leave no rhyme unused.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is kāmil, and every line rhymes in -iyah, the hāʾ held in pause; the print sets the final ه now with a sukūn, now bare. The first line repeats its rhyme word, ʿalāniyah, “in the open, public”, in both halves, as the opening line of a poem may rhyme its two halves. In the second line the subject of yudhīʿuhu, “discloses it”, is ḥālī, “my state”, held over into the second half; khafiya ʿalā, “to be hidden from”. al-ḥimā, “the protected ground”, the beloved's tribal pasture, left behind when the tribe moves on. bikum, “through you, on your account”. ghawr al-ḥashā, “the depths of the entrails”, the seat of the passions. fidāʾ, “ransom”: anā fidāʾuka, “I am your ransom”, would give my life for yours. muhja, “heart's blood, life”. insān al-ʿayn, literally “the little man of the eye”, is the pupil. In the seventh line the -hi of ʿalayhi most likely returns to love, al-hawā; the reading is not certain. hayhāta, “far from it!”. mā udhunī … wāʿiyah, “my ear is not heeding”: mā negates a nominal sentence, and its predicate, which Classical grammar of the Ḥijāz puts in the accusative, stands here in the pausal form of the rhyme. In the eighth line Budūr, disguised as Qamar al-Zamān and speaking to his bride, names her lost husband: Ḥayāt al-Nufūs hears the name she knows her husband by, and Budūr means the man himself. amāniyah is amāniya, “hopes”, plural of umniyya, with the hāʾ of pause. al-mulūk al-khāliya, “the kings gone by”: khāliya, “past, bygone”. In the tenth line ansā, “he made (people) forget”, wants its second object in the accusative, karama ibni Zāʾidata; the print points the phrase karamu ibnu Zāʾidati … wa-ḥilmu, with a damma on كرم, ابن and حلم and a kasra on زائدة, and that is kept. Ibn Zāʾida is Maʿn ibn Zāʾida, an Arab commander under the last Umayyads and the first ʿAbbāsids, proverbial for his generosity; Muʿāwiya, the first Umayyad caliph, was proverbial for his ḥilm, the forbearance of a ruler who will not be provoked. In the last line lawlā … lam adaʿ, “were it not for … I would not leave”: the answer is a negated jussive, without la-. al-qarīḍ, “verse”, a poet's word for poetry. min qāfiyah, “any rhyme”: min after the negative makes it “not a single one”. The verse is addressed to “you”, -ka, the beloved spoken to directly. The hamza of الْفَضَائِلَ, الْغَائِبِيْنَ, فِدَاءُ and زَائِدَةِ is printed; the print sets a bare alif without hamza in اُخْفِى, وَاَنَا, اَبَدًا, وَاَشْوَاقِيْ, اِلَيْهِمْ, اِنْسَانُهَا, اُذُنِيْ, وَاِنَّمَا, اَنَالُ, اَمَانِيَه, اَحَدٌ, اَنْسَى, الْاَنَامَ, الْاِطَالَةُ and اَدَعْ, and writes fī as فِى once; all are kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ نَهَضَتْ قَائِمَةً عَلَى أَقْدَامِهَا وَمَسَحَتْ دُمُوعَهَا وَ تَوَضَّأَتْ وَصَلَّتْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malikata Budūra nahaḍat qāʾimatan ʿalā aqdāmihā wa-masaḥat dumūʿahā wa-tawaḍḍaʾat wa-ṣallat
sentences.l: Then indeed the-Queen Budūr rose standing upon her-feet, and-wiped her-tears, and-performed-ablution and-prayed.
sentences.i: Then Queen Budūr rose to her feet, wiped away her tears, made her ablutions and prayed.
sentences.n: nahaḍat qāʾimatan ʿalā aqdāmihā, “she rose standing on her feet”, a stock fullness of phrase; qāʾimatan is a circumstantial accusative. The print sets the wa- of wa-tawaḍḍaʾat apart at the end of its line (و توضأت); it is kept as set. ṣallat, “she prayed”, from ṣallā. The ئ of قائمة and the hamza of توضأت are printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تُصَلِّي إِلَى أَنْ غَلَبَ النَّوْمُ عَلَى السِّتِّ حَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ فَنَامَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tuṣallī ilā an ghalaba al-nawmu ʿalā al-sitti Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi fa-nāmat
sentences.l: And-not she-ceased praying until that overcame the-sleep upon the-Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, and-she-slept.
sentences.i: She went on praying until sleep overcame the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs and she slept.
sentences.n: ghalaba ʿalā, “to overcome, get the better of”. The shadda of تصلّي is printed.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ وَرَقَدَتْ بِجَانِبِهَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾati al-sittu Budūru wa-raqadat bi-jānibihā ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And-came the-Lady Budūr and-lay-down at-her-side until the-morning.
sentences.i: Then the Lady Budūr came and lay down beside her until morning.
sentences.n: raqada, “to lie down, sleep”. bi-jānibihā, “at her side”: bi- is “at”. The hamza of جاءت is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَصَلَّتِ الصُّبْحَ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ الْمَمْلَكَةِ وَأَمَرَتْ وَنَهَتْ وَحَكَمَتْ وَعَدَلَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat wa-ṣallati al-ṣubḥa wa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyi al-mamlakati wa-amarat wa-nahat wa-ḥakamat wa-ʿadalat
sentences.l: Then she-rose and-prayed the-dawn, and-sat upon (the) throne (of) the-kingdom, and-commanded and-forbade and-judged and-was-just.
sentences.i: Then she rose and said the dawn prayer, and sat on the throne of the kingdom, and gave commands and prohibitions, and judged, and judged justly.
sentences.n: ṣallat al-ṣubḥa, “she prayed the dawn”, that is, the dawn prayer, ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ, named by its hour. ʿadala, “to act justly”.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihā
sentences.l: This (is) what was of her-affair.
sentences.i: So much for her.
sentences.n: The print sets mā kāna run together (ماكان) here and in the next sentence; it is kept as set.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ فَإِنَّهُ دَخَلَ عَلَى ابْنَتِهِ وَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ حَالِهَا فَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِجَمِيعِ مَا جَرَى لَهَا وَأَنْشَدَتْ لَهُ الشِّعْرَ الَّذِى قَالَتْهُ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-maliki Armānūsa fa-innahu dakhala ʿalā ibnatihi wa-saʾalahā ʿan ḥālihā fa-akhbarathu bi-jamīʿi mā jarā lahā wa-anshadat lahu al-shiʿra alladhī qālathu al-malikatu Budūru
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) King Armānūs, then-indeed-he went-in upon his-daughter and-asked-her about her-state; and-she-informed-him of-all what happened to-her, and-recited to-him the-verse which said-it the-Queen Budūr.
sentences.i: As for King Armānūs, he went in to his daughter and asked her how she fared, and she told him all that had happened to her and recited to him the verses Queen Budūr had spoken.
sentences.n: Armānūsa is diptote, so its genitive ends in -a. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to” someone in their room. akhbara … bi-, “to tell someone of”: bi- marks the matter told. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it befalls. anshada li-, “to recite to”: li- marks the hearer. alladhī qālathu, “which she said”: the -hu returns to al-shiʿr. The print writes alladhī as الذى. The hamza of سألها is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ يَا أَبِي مَارَأَيْتُ أَحَدًا أَكْثَرَ عَقْلًا وَحَيَاءً مِنْ زَوْجِي غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ يَبْكِي وَيَتَنَهَّدُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat yā abī mā raʾaytu aḥadan akthara ʿaqlan wa-ḥayāʾan min zawjī ghayra annahu yabkī wa-yatanahhadu
sentences.l: Then she-said: O my-father, not I-have-seen anyone more (in) sense and-modesty than my-husband, except that-he weeps and-sighs.
sentences.i: Then she said, “Father, I have never seen anyone with more good sense and modesty than my husband, only he weeps and sighs.”
sentences.n: mā raʾaytu, “I have not seen”, set run together in the print (مارأيت), kept as set. akthara ʿaqlan wa-ḥayāʾan, “more in sense and modesty”: the accusatives ʿaqlan and ḥayāʾan say in what respect he is “more” (tamyīz). ghayra anna, “except that, only”. tanahhada, Form V, “to sigh”; its shadda is printed, as is the hamza of رأيت and of حياء.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَبُوهَا يَا بِنْتِي اصْبِرِي عَلَيْهِ فَمَا بَقِيَ غَيْرُ هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā abūhā yā bintī iṣbirī ʿalayhi fa-mā baqiya ghayru hādhihi al-laylati al-thālithati
sentences.l: And-said to-her her-father: O my-daughter, be-patient with-him, for-not remained other-than this the-night the-third.
sentences.i: Her father said to her, “My daughter, bear with him: there is only this third night left.
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here: hādhihi, “this”. ṣabara ʿalā, “to be patient with, bear with”. fa-mā baqiya ghayru, “for there remains nothing but”: ghayru is the subject of baqiya. The king speaks as if three nights were the term a bridegroom is allowed, and this is the last of them; the text has not said so before.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ لَمْ يَدْخُلْ بِكِ وَيُزِيلْ بَكَارَتَكِ يَكُنْ لَنَا مَعَهُ رَأْيٌ وَتَدْبِيرٌ وَأَخْلَعُهُ مِنَ الْمُلْكِ وَأَنْفِيهِ عَنْ بِلَادِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-in lam yadkhul biki wa-yuzīl bakārataki yakun lanā maʿahu raʾyun wa-tadbīrun wa-akhlaʿuhu mina al-mulki wa-anfīhi ʿan bilādinā
sentences.l: So-if not he-goes-in with-you and-removes your-virginity, will-be to-us with-him a-view and-a-plan, and-I-depose-him from the-kingship and-banish-him from our-lands.
sentences.i: If he does not go in to you and take your maidenhead, we shall have our own mind about him and our own plan: I shall depose him from the throne and banish him from our country.”
sentences.n: dakhala bi-, “to go in with” a bride, that is, to consummate the marriage: bi- here is “with”. yuzīl, “he removes”, from azāla, Form IV: after lam the Classical jussive would be yuzil, with the long vowel shortened, but the print keeps the ī (ويزيل), as the later language does; it is kept. bakāra, “virginity”. yakun, jussive, as the answer to in, “if”. lanā maʿahu raʾyun, “we will have a view regarding him”, a mild way of saying they will deal with him. wa-akhlaʿuhu … wa-anfīhi, “and I will depose him … and banish him”: the king passes from “we” to “I”, and from the jussive to the plain indicative, as the spoken language would. khalaʿa, “to take off (a garment)”, and so “to depose” a ruler. nafā, “to banish”. The hamza of رأي is printed.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ مَعَ ابْنَتِهِ عَلَى هٰذَا الْكَلَامِ وَأَضْمَرَ عَلَى هٰذَا الرَّأْيِ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa maʿa ibnatihi ʿalā hādhā al-kalāmi wa-aḍmara ʿalā hādhā al-raʾyi
sentences.l: And-he-agreed with his-daughter upon this the-speech, and-resolved-secretly upon this the-view.
sentences.i: So he agreed with his daughter on this, and inwardly settled on that course.
sentences.n: ittafaqa maʿa … ʿalā, Form VIII, “to agree with someone on something”. aḍmara, Form IV, “to conceal in one's mind, resolve on in secret”; Classical takes its object directly, and ʿalā here is the later usage, after ʿazama ʿalā, “to resolve on”. The hamza of الرأي is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ. The print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; they are kept as set.
